title: 1972 Sacramento Canadair Sabre accident

agencies.name: National Transportation Safety Board
agencies.report_title: Aircraft Accident Report - Spectrum Air, Inc., Sabre Mark 5, N275X, Sacramento Executive Airport

summary: A Canadair Sabre Mk. 5 flown by pilot Richard L. Bingham failed to gain sufficient altitude during takeoff on runway 30 from Sacramento Executive Airport during the Golden West Sport Aviation Air Show. With nose over-rotated, aircraft overran runway, external fuel tanks ruptured and ignited, crossed Freeport Boulevard before striking Farrell's Ice Cream Parlor. Twenty-two people on ground were killed.
probable_cause: The probable cause of this accident was the overrotation of the aircraft and subsequent derogation of the performance capability. The overrotation was the result of inadequate pilot proficiency in the aircraft and misleading visual cues.

factors.evidence: Bingham had fewer than four hours of flying time in Sabre Mark 5; his most recent jet experience was primarily in Lear Jet as second-in-command (p. 7-8)
Pilot applied excessive nose-up control, rotating to 17° ANU compared to 5° in a normal Sabre takeoff; eyewitnesses and movie analysis confirmed nose was over-rotated (p. 14-19)

F-86 Sabre has dangerous handling characteristic upon takeoff if nose is raised prematurely; the aircraft's elevator power at slow speeds allows high angles of attack before flying speed is attained, with insufficient thrust to overcome induced drag (p. 18)
Aircraft overran runway at approximately 150 mph, struck earthen berm and ripped through perimeter fence (p. 6)
Two external underwing fuel tanks ruptured and ignited creating massive fireball; fire trail followed aircraft across Freeport Boulevard into the building (p. 13)

events.text: Sabre takeoff commenced on runway 30 from Sacramento Executive Airport
At approximately 105 knots, pilot applied back pressure to raise nosewheel off runway
Initial lift-off occurred at 2,800-2,900 feet from end of runway at 124 knots, 11° nose-up attitude
Aircraft reached 130.5 knots and 15.5° nose-up attitude but acceleration stopped and speed began decreasing; aircraft 7 feet above ground
Pilot felt and heard unusual vibration; instinctively lowered nose
Aircraft settled back to runway at approximately 3,700 feet at 128 knots, 10° nose-up attitude
Pilot resumed takeoff attitude for second attempt; speed increased to approximately 137 knots with 16.5° nose-up attitude
Second lift-off occurred at approximately 5,005 feet from end of runway; pilot realized aircraft would not fly
Pilot began rejected takeoff procedure; closed throttle and touched down
Aircraft hit perimeter fence and became airborne again at approximately 800 feet from end of runway; crossed Freeport Boulevard
Pilot shut off fuel switch and shielded face with right arm; unable to control aircraft
Aircraft crashed through ice cream parlor; external fuel tanks ruptured and ignited; aircraft destroyed by impact and fire

recommendations.text: Limit the issuance of experimental certificates to those aircraft and operations that are truly experimental in nature and reclassify the other activities listed in FAR 21.191 in a manner that will permit more selective regulatory control without unduly inhibiting the promotion of aviation.
Establish pilot experience, transition, and proficiency standards applicable to the operation of all high-performance surplus military aircraft, reciprocating as well as turbine engine powered.

Establish additional airshow separation criteria applicable to persons and property in other than designated spectator areas to insure that the overall suitability of an airport for airshows is taken into account.

Include in the guidelines dealing with compatible land use planning around airports, consideration for the safety of persons and property on the ground, and use the controls available in the Airport Development Aid Program to insure compliance.

Establish guidelines that will assist airport managers in setting limitations on the utilization of runways where existing environmental encroachment and runway length combine to create a high risk level for certain aircraft operations.

safety_changes: FAA issued General Notice (GENOT) on November 9, 1972, establishing new standards for civil certification, operation, and maintenance of military surplus jet airplanes
Enhanced pilot qualification requirements for surplus military aircraft operations, including mandatory checkout and recent pilot-in-command experience
FAA tightened rules on ex-military jet operations and experimental aircraft certification procedures

notes: Pilot had 3.5-7.3 hours total in Sabre; most jet experience in Lear Jet
Aircraft was ex-military F-86 surplus sold to private operator
Movie analysis provided precise altitude and attitude data for timeline
Visual illusions at Sacramento runway (vs Oakland) contributed to overrotation
